opus-5.5.text:
I think the important thing is not to picture a single moment where robots suddenly "work." It's much more like a flywheel. Once a robot is good enough to do something useful, even something fairly narrow, you can deploy it. Deployment gives you data, the data makes the system better, and a better system can be deployed more broadly. So the real question is when that flywheel starts spinning, not when you get a fully general home robot that does everything.

My sense is that we're actually pretty close to that starting point. With the foundation models we've been building, robots that use vision-language models as a backbone and are trained on large amounts of diverse robot data, we're seeing behaviors that would have seemed out of reach a few years ago. Folding laundry, cleaning up a kitchen, handling objects the robot has never seen before. They're not perfect, but they're good enough that you can imagine putting them in real settings with some human oversight.

If you made me put numbers on it, I'd say that within something like one to two years we'll see robots doing genuinely useful work in at least some real-world deployments. Then, maybe within about five years, you get to something approaching the kind of broadly capable robot people imagine, one that can handle most of the tasks in a home or a workplace with a reasonable amount of instruction. I wouldn't be shocked if it were faster or slower, but single-digit years is how I think about it.

The reason I'm relatively optimistic is that the hard part was never just the mechanical hardware. It was getting the generality: common sense, the ability to adapt, to recover from mistakes. That's exactly what these large pretrained models bring in. Robotics doesn't have to solve all of intelligence from scratch anymore. It can stand on the shoulders of what's been learned from web-scale data, and then the robot-specific part is learning the physical skills on top of that.

The other piece people underestimate is that a robot doesn't need to be fully autonomous to be useful. A person can work alongside it, correct it, give it instructions. That's actually how you'd want the early phase to go, because those interactions are themselves a source of learning. So I think "autonomous robots becoming useful" will look less like a product launch and more like a gradual expansion, where the scope of what they can do on their own keeps growing as they gain experience.

r001.rationale: It says robots can be deployed in real settings once they are good enough to do useful work, even in a narrow role.

r002.rationale: It explains that deployment produces data and experience that make the system better.

r003.rationale: It identifies the key milestone as the flywheel starting to spin, rather than achieving a fully general robot.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "useful," and I try to be careful about that because the question has a way of collapsing into either hype or pessimism.

The way I think about it is that there's a kind of flywheel that needs to get started. With language models, the data was already there. The internet existed, people had been writing things for decades, and once the methods got good enough, you could just scale on that. Robotics doesn't have that. There's no internet of robot experience. So the hard part isn't really the algorithms, or at least not only the algorithms. The hard part is that you need robots out in the world doing things in order to get the data that makes robots good at doing things in the world. And that's circular, which is why it's been slow.

What's changed in the last couple of years is that we've figured out how to get that loop going with a lot less data than people expected. Pretraining on diverse robot data across many embodiments, combining it with vision-language models that already understand a lot about the world semantically, and then fine-tuning on fairly modest amounts of task-specific data. You get something that generalizes in ways that would have seemed implausible five years ago. A robot that's never been in your kitchen can fold laundry or bus a table, not perfectly, but recognizably.

So my timeline view is something like: in the near term, meaning the next couple of years, I think we'll see robots that are economically useful in narrow but real settings. Not fully general, but general enough that you don't have to re-engineer the whole system every time the environment changes a little. That's the threshold that matters, because that's when deployment stops being a research project and starts being a product. And once it's a product, the data starts flowing, and then you get the flywheel.

The longer-term question, the "when does a robot do everything a person can do in the home" question, I'm much less confident about. I'd guess it's not decades, but I also don't think anyone really knows. What I'd push back on is the idea that there's some fundamental barrier. Every time I've looked at what seemed like a fundamental barrier in this field, it turned out to be a data problem or a scale problem in disguise. That makes me optimistic, but it also makes me think the timeline is really going to be set by how fast we can get robots out there collecting experience, more than by any single breakthrough in the lab.

r001.rationale: It predicts economically useful robots in narrow real-world settings within the next couple of years, once they are competent enough to deploy as products.

r002.rationale: It says product deployment causes data to flow and that robots improve by collecting experience in the world.

r003.rationale: It presents the key milestone as starting a deployment-driven data flywheel, and says the timeline depends on how quickly robots get deployed to collect experience.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by useful. There are already robots doing useful things in fairly structured environments. The harder question is when you can put a robot into a new environment, tell it what you want, and expect it to get the job done without an engineer standing next to it.

I’m more optimistic about that than I used to be, but I’d separate being able to demonstrate a task from being able to deploy it. If a robot does something correctly nine times out of ten, that can make for an impressive demonstration. If it’s doing that task hundreds of times a day, you have a system that needs constant help. Reliability, and especially the ability to recover when something goes wrong, matters enormously.

One thing I would watch is whether deployments start producing data that makes the next deployment easier. You could imagine a robot doing a relatively narrow job, asking a person for help occasionally, and learning from those interventions. If that process works, you have a way to improve the system through actual use. If every new installation requires a separate engineering project, progress will be much slower.

So I’d expect useful applications to emerge incrementally, with constrained tasks coming first. A robot that can handle essentially anything in your home is a much higher bar. I’m reluctant to attach a precise year to that, because the timeline depends on whether we get that learning process working at scale.

r001.rationale: It says useful applications will emerge incrementally, with constrained tasks coming first, and notes that robots already perform useful tasks in structured settings.

r002.rationale: It identifies deployment data and learning from human interventions as ways to make later deployments easier and improve the system.

r003.rationale: It says the timeline depends on whether deployments produce a learning process that works at scale, framing that cycle as the milestone to watch.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by useful. We already have robots doing useful things in fairly structured environments. The harder question is when we’ll have robots that you can put into a new environment, tell them what you want, and expect them to figure it out without a team of engineers setting everything up.

I’m fairly optimistic that we’ll see more of that over the next few years, initially in settings where the tasks are somewhat constrained and where failures are recoverable. But I’m much less confident about putting a date on a robot that can do essentially anything in your home. There’s a big difference between demonstrating a task and doing it reliably every day.

To me, the important thing is whether we can get a learning process going where deploying robots produces data, that data improves the system, and the improved system can do more things and therefore collect more useful data. If we can close that loop, progress could become quite fast. If every new deployment requires substantial manual engineering, it’s going to be much slower. So I would pay more attention to whether that loop is working than to any particular impressive demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response predicts broader real-world use over the next few years in constrained settings, once robots can handle tasks usefully without extensive setup.

r002.rationale: It says deployment produces data that improves the system, enabling more capabilities and more useful data.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes whether the deployment and learning loop is working over impressive demonstrations, but does not frame that as the milestone instead of development being complete.
